learner_answer: Three regions in order: first a metadata header with the architecture, layer and head counts, context length and the tokenizer; then a tensor index giving each tensor's name, shape, numeric type and byte offset; then the tensor data itself, the weights, aligned for memory mapping.
rationale: All three rubric points hit (metadata header, tensor index, tensor data) in the correct order.

learner_answer: A GGUF starts with a metadata header holding the architecture and the tokenizer, and the rest of the file is the tensor data: the weights, laid out so the operating system can memory-map them.
rationale: Fluent and correct as far as it goes, but omits the tensor index entirely — two of three points. Classic missing-one-point case.

learner_answer: It contains the training code, the training data, and the weights.
rationale: Confident but wrong on every point: a GGUF carries no code and no training data. Only the vague mention of weights is salvageable.

learner_answer: About 14 GB. Weight memory is parameter count times bytes per parameter: 7 billion parameters times 2 bytes for a 16-bit weight gives 14 GB, plus a little metadata.
rationale: Correct figure and correct rule stated — the single rubric point is fully hit.

learner_answer: About 7 GB, since a 7B model always takes one byte per parameter no matter the precision.
rationale: Confidently wrong: applies the 8-bit rule to 16-bit weights and asserts precision is irrelevant, contradicting the rule the question asks for.

learner_answer: The four terms are the weights (about 7.5 GB for a 13B at 4-bit), the KV cache at the context length actually used (about 2 GB at 8k tokens), compute buffers for in-flight activations, and whatever the OS and desktop were already using. You keep 10-15% free because allocators fragment, drivers reserve unreported memory, and a context that grows past plan has nowhere to go.
rationale: All four budget terms named plus the headroom reasoning — every rubric point hit.

learner_answer: Weights, the KV cache for your context length, and the compute buffers. Headroom matters because drivers reserve memory they don't report and the context can grow beyond what you planned.
rationale: Fluent with a good headroom explanation but misses the fourth term — memory already used by the OS and desktop. Three of four points.

learner_answer: kv_bytes = 2 x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes_per_elem x context_tokens. The 2 is for keys and values; every layer keeps its own cache; kv_heads is the key/value head count, which GQA makes smaller than the query heads; head_dim is each head's vector width; bytes_per_elem is 2 for FP16; and every token in the context, prompt included, adds one entry.
rationale: Formula reproduced exactly and every factor correctly identified — all rubric points hit.

learner_answer: kv_bytes = layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes_per_elem x context_tokens. Layers because the cache exists per layer, kv_heads for the key/value heads, head_dim for the vector width, bytes for the element size, and tokens for the context length.
rationale: Five of six factors identified but the leading 2 is missing — the answer never accounts for keys and values being two tensors. A real conceptual gap, not a typo.

learner_answer: The cache stores one key and one value vector per token in every layer, so its size is proportional to the token count and doubles when the context doubles. The weights are fixed learned parameters that get read once per generated token regardless of how long the conversation is, so their memory doesn't change.
rationale: Both rubric points hit: per-token cache scaling and context-independent weight memory.

learner_answer: The cache has to hold every token's attention state, so more tokens means proportionally more cache. I don't know why the weights stay the same size.
rationale: First point hit, second explicitly missing — half the mechanism explained.

learner_answer: The working set — 20 GB of weights plus the KV cache and buffers — is larger than 16 GB of RAM, so the OS evicts mapped pages. Since every generated token re-reads essentially every weight, evicted pages are faulted back from disk continuously, and as the KV cache grows the pressure and the slowdown get worse. Remedies from most to least effective: use a smaller model or smaller quant so the working set fits in RAM, shorten the context to reduce cache pressure, add RAM. Swap is not a remedy — it makes every token stall on disk.
rationale: Mechanism fully explained (working set exceeds RAM, per-token weight sweep causes refaults, growth worsens it) and the remedy ranking matches the official answer.

learner_answer: The model is too big for the machine so it has to swap to disk, which is slow. The fix is to add more swap space so the thrashing stops.
rationale: Gestures at the size problem but misidentifies the mechanism (mmap page refaults, not conventional swap) and prescribes a remedy the lesson explicitly calls counterproductive.

learner_answer: Quantization changes only how weights are stored: 16-bit floats become low-bit codes with per-block scales, expanded back to full precision during the matmul. The architecture, the arithmetic precision, and the KV cache and activations are all unchanged.
rationale: Both halves correct: what changes (storage encoding) and the full list of what does not (architecture, arithmetic, cache/activations).

learner_answer: Q4 is the nominal 4-bit width, about half a byte per weight. K marks the k-quants, llama.cpp's block family where superblocks share a higher-precision scale. M is the size mix: sensitive tensors like the embeddings and output projection get stored wider, so the file averages about 4.8 bits per weight.
rationale: All three parts of the code decoded correctly — every rubric point hit.

learner_answer: Q4 means 4 bits per weight. M is the medium size variant. K is some kernel-level compression trick, I think.
rationale: Q4 essentially right, M partially right, K guessed wrong — one solid point of three with a confident misfire on the rest.

learner_answer: Each bit removed doubles the spacing between representable values in a block. At 8 bits there are 256 levels, generous for weight distributions, so rounding error is tiny. At 3 bits there are only 8 levels, the per-weight error is large, and it accumulates across the hundreds of matmuls a token passes through, concentrated where the model was already uncertain.
rationale: The full mechanism: doubling spacing per bit, 256 vs 8 levels, and error accumulation — both rubric points hit.

learner_answer: 8-bit keeps almost all the precision so the model is basically unchanged, while 3-bit compresses much harder and the quality drops noticeably.
rationale: Directionally right but mechanism-free: no mention of representable levels, rounding error, or accumulation. A restatement of the question's premise, not an explanation.

learner_answer: Long reasoning chains, arithmetic, and rare-fact recall degrade first. They all depend on narrow margins where the right continuation barely outranks plausible wrong ones, so rounding noise erodes them before fluent, well-redundant generation.
rationale: Three of the four capabilities plus the margin mechanism — fluent but missing instruction following over long prompts.

learner_answer: A 13B has enough redundancy to absorb 4-bit rounding error and still beat a 7B on most tasks; the 8-bit 7B can't recover the capability gap that six billion extra parameters buy. The trade stops below about 3 bits, where the per-weight error gets so large that even a big model loses coherence and the smaller, more precise model wins again.
rationale: Both rubric points hit: redundancy absorbing error and the ~3-bit floor where the trade reverses.

learner_answer: The cache grows linearly with context while weights stay fixed, so at long context the cache dominates the budget and halving its element size saves gigabytes; at short context it saves little. The cost is attention quality over long ranges — small at 8 bits, visibly worse at 4, because long-range attention is exactly where key precision matters.
rationale: Both rubric points hit: why long context makes cache quantization matter, and the quality cost profile.

learner_answer: Subtract the KV cache at 8k context (computed from the candidate's layers, KV heads, head width and element size) from the 16 GB to get the weight allowance. Take the largest model that fits the allowance at the highest bit width, preferring K-quants and imatrix files below 4 bits. Recheck that weights plus cache plus buffers still leave 10-15% free, stepping down a quant or model size if not. Then sanity-check the finalist on your own prompts.
rationale: The full procedure in order: budget minus cache, largest fitting model at highest width, headroom recheck, task-level sanity check.
Blank answer: no rubric point can be credited, quality 0 by definition.
